name: Why antibiotics do not work on viruses
headline: Why antibiotics do not work for colds, flu and most coughs, and what the NHS says instead
summary: Antibiotics act on bacteria, not viruses, so the NHS says they do not help colds, flu or most coughs and sore throats.
keyPoints: The NHS says antibiotics do not work against viral infections, which include the common cold, flu and most coughs and sore throats.
NHS England says overuse of antibiotics in recent years has played a major part in antibiotic resistance, which can lead to treatment failure.
NICE describes acute cough as usually self-limiting, getting better within about 3 to 4 weeks without antibiotics.
One NHS page notes that if antibiotics are stopped early, bacteria can become resistant to them.
For flu, NHS pages describe 999 for severe difficulty breathing, and an urgent GP or NHS 111 route for people who feel short of breath.

body.heading: What is the difference between bacteria and viruses?
body.body: Antibiotics are medicines used to treat or prevent some bacterial infections. NHS inform says they kill bacteria or stop them from reproducing and spreading. Antibiotics do not work against infections caused by viruses. NHS inform lists the common cold, flu, most coughs and most sore throats among these viral illnesses. Penicillins, the group that includes amoxicillin, are antibiotics, so they act on bacteria only.

body.heading: Why do antibiotics not help colds, flu and coughs?
body.body: The NHS common cold page says GPs do not recommend antibiotics for colds, because they will not relieve symptoms or speed up recovery. NHS inform says the same about flu. NICE guidance on acute cough describes the illness as usually self-limiting, which means it gets better, within about 3 to 4 weeks, without antibiotics. NICE also notes that antibiotics make little difference to how long a cough lasts.

body.heading: What is antibiotic resistance?
body.body: Antibiotic resistance means that a strain of bacteria no longer responds to treatment with one or more types of antibiotic. NHS England says overuse of antibiotics in recent years has played a major part in it. It says resistance can lead to treatment failure, repeat GP appointments, hospital admissions and more. The UKHSA campaign Keep Antibiotics Working, listed on a Department of Health and Social Care campaign page, gives three core messages: antibiotics are not for colds and flu, which are caused by viruses; antibiotics are taken as directed by the prescriber; and leftover antibiotics are not saved, because they may not work properly and could make the problem worse.

body.heading: Should an antibiotic course always be finished?
body.body: NHS sources describe stopping a course early as a risk: one NHS page notes that if antibiotics are stopped early, bacteria can become resistant to them.

body.heading: What helps with a viral illness?
body.body: NHS guidance on flu describes rest, fluids and paracetamol or ibuprofen for symptoms. A local NHS page on colds says most colds do not need a visit to the GP and that pharmacists can advise on suitable medicines. NICE lists honey as a self-care option for acute cough in people older than one year, although it describes the evidence as weak.

body.heading: What side effects can antibiotics have?
body.body: NHS trust leaflets list feeling sick, vomiting, diarrhoea and bloating as the most common side effects of antibiotics. Allergic reactions are rarer but can be serious, with swelling of the face or tongue and difficulty breathing as warning signs. One leaflet says anyone with difficulty breathing, dizziness or collapse should call 999. Severe diarrhoea can be a symptom of C. difficile infection, and the same leaflet says to contact the GP if diarrhoea continues after the course ends. A pharmacist or GP can answer questions about a particular medicine.

body.heading: When does the NHS say to get help urgently?
body.body: NHS inform says to call 999 for severe difficulty breathing. NHS England's flu page lists sudden chest pain, severe breathing trouble and coughing up blood as reasons for emergency care, by calling 999 or going to A&E. NHS inform adds lips or skin turning blue or grey, and being harder to wake than usual. NHS flu pages place people who feel short of breath, and people at higher risk of complications, in an urgent group for a same-day GP appointment or NHS 111. Questions that are not urgent can go to a pharmacist or the GP.
